title: Chapter 1 - The hesitation of facing Death
description:
At first, we just wanted to know more about Death. So we went to the Thanh Nhàn Funeral Home, hoping to hear the stories of those who work surrounded by Death. But looking at their uneasy faces, perhaps we had been a little too abrupt. Maybe this culture is still not yet ready to talk about death, no matter how familiar with it they are.

We had to emphasize many times that we wanted to hear the story from his perspective, a man who had worked in funeral services for years, but he kept brushing it off. "We can’t share anything about this" "You should look it up on the internet or ask those people over there," he said, pointing to one of the clients. 

Death seemed like a bad omen to be hidden and avoided, not something to be examined as a human experience, which is what we were trying to do.

media.caption: An interview with someone in the death-care service

title: Chapter 2 - The language of Death
description:
But the rejection did not stop us. If anything, because this was something so few people dared to think about, we grew even more curious and more committed to our subject. Fortunately, we met Ms. H, a funeral florist, and caught an interesting insight: each flower color at a funeral carries its own meaning, as married people with yellow and young adults go with white ones. Eventually, the family orders whatever they wish.

In other words, beyond gratitude and filial devotion, flowers are a gentle announcement to tell the community who this person was, and where they stood among the living. And so, from the very first petal, Death is no longer the sole property of the one who has gone. It becomes a shared space of ritual, belonging to those who remain.

We realized that in a culture as deeply collective as Vietnam, so long rooted in village ties and communal bonds, it would be an oversight to approach Death as a solitary journey. From this moment, we decided to look at Death through the lens of the funeral, a thread powerfully connecting the one who has left with their family and community.

title: Chapter 3 - Sacred connections 1 - A funeral at home
description:
Location: Thi Ông village, Hải Lăng district, Quảng Trị province (Private Ancestral Hall)
At Vietnamese funerals, there is always noise and always crowds. Those who come to pay their respects bow before the departed, the family bows back, and this process would last for many days. In those exchanged gestures of reverence, an invisible thread is woven between souls.

At my grandfather's funeral, nestled among the layered mountains of Quảng Trị, in the central part of the country, the mourners included people who had never met him, or perhaps only once or twice, the family of in-laws, the friends of someone in the house. I found myself wondering: who had they come for?

Yet their presence was a quiet affirmation that our family would not grieve alone. And so, in the way that only death can, my grandfather's passing became something unexpectedly tender, a space where we were drawn closer together, and held more firmly than before.

title: Chapter 4 - Sacred connections 2 - The Burial
description:
Location: Chứa Chan Mountain, Xuân Lộc village, Đồng Nai province (Family cemetery)
It takes a village to raise a child. Watching the procession carry him through his final steps, all the way to Chứa Chan moutain, I thought, it also takes a village to let someone go in peace. That peace comes from being held by a community, all the way to the very last moment. Hundreds of people walking through village roads, following a single hearse, is an act of belonging. A quiet, collective declaration that you were ours, and we were yours.

The one who has passed does not fall immediately into the abyss of forgetting but is carried on the shoulders of neighbors, under the gaze of an entire community. Lifted, one last time, by the people who knew them. That is the most beautiful farewell a society can offer its human life.

title: Chapter 5 - Sacred connections 3 - Cooking together at a funeral
description:
Location: Quới Điền Cultural House, Quới Điền village, Vĩnh Long province
Strangely, somewhere among this country's funerals, in the Mekong Delta, laughter still rises. Neighbors gather to cook, to eat, to drink, to sing and more. This is simply how death is held in the land of rivers and water. They stay beside one another to share the weight of grief, or perhaps so the one who has passed may rest in peace, or perhaps for no reason at all, only because this is what they have always done, and always known. Whatever the reason may be, something between them grows stronger than it has ever been.

Despite the controversies this stirs, we still believe that laughter is not indifference or disrespect toward those who are gone. It is a quiet defiance against Death. A gentle healing of wounds that are shared by all. A rekindling of bonds that seemed, for a moment, to have been broken. Life, quietly, continues on, even in the very space where death has come to rest.

title: Chapter 6 - Sacred connections 4 - Bồ Đề Pagoda
description:
"Return to the Buddha." "Return to God." This is what Death means to a believer. Religion offers them a sense of belonging, a shelter that follows them all the way to the other side of life.

At a funeral, the devout find a quietness within their grief. Amid the murmur of sutras along the banks of the Red River, the individuals merge into something larger than themselves. Prayer is no longer a solitary cry from the heart, but a resonance that voices braided together into one. Within this spiritual land, sorrow is parceled out, shared among many, until the weight of loss becomes something the human soul can barely hold.

title: Chapter 7 - Let Death walk along with our existence - Bồ Đề Cemetery
description:
Nestled within the same grounds as Bồ Đề Pagoda, the graves press gently against one another, forming a quiet little neighborhood of their own. Across this country, or even across this world, solitary graves are rare. Even in stillness, people remain and wish to remain a part of something.

We hope that after following this map, if someone ever asks you about Death, you will feel a little less lost and know that it is not some distant story belonging to those in another realm. Because funerals, or Death, are a shared story, for both of those who leave and those who stay behind.

This project began as an effort to ease your fear of Death, or more precisely, the grief that Death carries with it. Not so that you might speak of Death more lightly, but so that you know: we are not alone on this journey.

title: Chapter 8 - Is there a twist?  - City Funeral Home
description:
But not every funeral is filled with crowds. Urbanization has narrowed our homes, leaving little room for the kind of farewell that spills into the street. Individual freedom has quietly crept into the fabric of community life, and neighbors have grown hesitant to impose on one another. So more and more, people turn to funeral homes to hold their grief. Will funerals one day have no place for the old village? Or has the village simply changed its shape with friends, colleagues, and relationships of modern social life slowly taking the place of the neighbors who once stood at the gate? 

Death in the city may feel quieter now. But the longing to be seen, to be mourned, to be carried home by a community, that remains as eternal as death itself.
